title: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)
subtitle: From RLHF to a simple preference loss, with Python labs
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: DPO (Rafailov et al., NeurIPS 2023) derived step by step: preference data and Bradley-Terry, the KL-regularised objective and its optimal policy, the loss, its gradient, implementation with sequence log-probabilities, choosing beta, and later variants (background). Theory plus Python labs.

chapters.title: From RLHF to DPO

maps.title: DPO
links: DPO | introduced by | Rafailov et al. 2023
DPO | replaces | Reward model plus RL

summary: Direct Preference Optimization, DPO, is a way to align a language model with human preferences using a simple loss on pairs of responses, one preferred and one rejected. It was introduced by Rafael Rafailov and colleagues at Stanford, NeurIPS 2023.

The usual route, RLHF, trains a reward model and then uses reinforcement learning such as PPO. DPO shows that, under the standard assumptions, the same goal can be reached by training the language model directly with a binary cross-entropy loss.
No separate reward model and no sampling loop are needed.
This course derives the loss step by step and builds each part in small Python labs.

glossary.def: A prompt with a chosen (preferred) response and a rejected one.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback.
A frozen copy of the starting model.
The reward that the policy itself defines: beta times the log-ratio to the reference.
A coefficient controlling how far the policy may move from the reference.
The loss for a yes-or-no prediction.

keyPoints: DPO: Rafailov, Sharma, Mitchell, Ermon, Manning and Finn, NeurIPS 2023.
Input: triples (x, y_w, y_l) with a winner and a loser.
Loss: -log sigmoid(beta (log pi/pi_ref (y_w) - log pi/pi_ref (y_l))).
No reward model, no RL sampling during training.
It assumes the Bradley-Terry model of preferences.
It needs log-probabilities from the policy and the frozen reference.

items: ELI5. RLHF teaches a model what people like through a judge and a long training loop. DPO says: skip the judge. Show the model pairs of answers, good and bad, and nudge it directly toward the good one.

A language model trained on text can write fluently but does not know what people prefer. To align it, the standard pipeline of RLHF has three stages. Fine-tune on good examples. Train a reward model on human comparisons.
Then optimise the language model against the reward model with reinforcement learning, with a penalty that keeps it close to the starting model.

That last stage is heavy. It samples from the model during training, it needs the reward model, a value model and a reference model in memory, and it is sensitive to hyperparameters. The question behind DPO is whether all that is necessary.

The DPO paper's answer is no. Its key observation is that the RL objective used in RLHF has a closed-form optimal policy, and that this relation can be turned around: the reward can be written in terms of the policy.
Once the reward is expressed through the policy, the preference-learning step for the reward model becomes a loss on the policy itself.

This is a binary classification loss. For each pair it asks: does the policy, relative to the reference, favour the winner over the loser? Training increases the log-probability ratio of winners and decreases that of losers. That is all.
It can be implemented in a few lines on top of ordinary supervised fine-tuning code.

A note on sources. This course follows the DPO paper and standard descriptions of it. Later variants and comparisons are marked as background knowledge. The labs use tiny numerical examples, not a real language model.

chapters.title: Preference data and the Bradley-Terry model

maps.title: Preferences
links: Sigmoid | converts | Reward gaps to probabilities

summary: Human feedback usually comes as comparisons: given two responses, which is better? The Bradley-Terry model turns this into probability. If response A has reward r_A and B has r_B, the chance that A is preferred is the sigmoid of the reward gap.

A reward model is trained by maximising the log-likelihood of the observed choices. RLHF does this as a separate stage. DPO reuses the same likelihood but with the reward expressed through the policy.
The labs compute sigmoid, preference probabilities and the log-likelihood of a dataset.

glossary.def: p(A beats B) = sigmoid(r_A - r_B).
sigma(z) = 1 / (1 + exp(-z)); maps any number into (0, 1).
log sigma(z): the log-probability of the observed choice.
The difference r_w - r_l between winner and loser.
The sum of log-probabilities of the data.
How often different people make the same choice.

keyPoints: p(y_w beats y_l) = sigmoid(r(y_w) - r(y_l)).
sigmoid(0) = 0.5; large positive gap gives probability near 1.
Training a reward model: minimise -log sigmoid(r_w - r_l).
Only reward differences matter, not absolute values.
Real labels are noisy; Bradley-Terry treats them as probabilistic.
The model assumes preferences come from a single underlying score.

items: ELI5. Preference data is pairs: this answer is better than that one. Bradley-Terry turns this into odds, like a ranking in a tournament where each item has a strength and stronger ones win more often.

Asking people to give a response a score from one to ten is unreliable: different people use the scale differently. Asking which of two responses is better is easier and more consistent. That is why preference data usually takes the form of comparisons.

To learn from comparisons we need a model of how they arise. The Bradley-Terry model, from 1952, supposes each item has a hidden score, and the chance that one beats another depends on the gap between scores. The bigger the gap, the more reliably the higher-scored item wins.

Look at the shape of the sigmoid. At zero it is one half: equal scores, a coin toss. For a gap of two it is about 0.88. For a gap of five, about 0.99. Because only the difference matters, adding the same number to all rewards changes nothing. This invariance will be important in the derivation.

Given a dataset of pairs, the reward model is trained by maximum likelihood: pick the scores that make the observed winners as probable as possible. Equivalently, minimise the negative log-likelihood. This is the classic first stage of RLHF.
DPO keeps exactly this loss. What changes is what plays the role of the reward. The next chapters show that the policy itself can define it.

chapters.title: The KL-regularised objective and its optimal policy

maps.title: Optimal policy
links: RLHF objective | maximises | Reward minus KL
KL term | keeps | Policy near reference
Optimal policy | is | Reference times exp of reward
Reward | defines | A tilt of the reference

summary: The RL stage of RLHF maximises expected reward while keeping the policy near the reference model: a reward term minus beta times the KL divergence from the reference. This problem has a closed-form solution.
The optimal policy is the reference policy reweighted by the exponential of reward over beta, then normalised. Responses with high reward get more probability, with beta controlling how strongly.
The normaliser, called the partition function, is expensive to compute for language models. DPO's trick, in the next chapter, is that it will cancel.

glossary.def: E[r(x, y)] - beta * KL(pi || pi_ref).
pi*(y|x) = pi_ref(y|x) exp(r(x,y)/beta) / Z(x).
Z(x) = sum_y pi_ref(y|x) exp(r(x,y)/beta), the normaliser.
Reweighting a distribution by an exponential factor.
Here beta plays the role of a temperature on the reward.
The set of responses with nonzero probability.

keyPoints: max over pi of E_{y~pi}[r(x,y)] - beta KL(pi(.|x) || pi_ref(.|x)).
Solution: pi*(y|x) = pi_ref(y|x) exp(r(x,y)/beta) / Z(x).
beta -> infinity: pi* approaches pi_ref; beta -> 0: pi* concentrates on the highest-reward response.
Z(x) sums over all possible responses, which is intractable for language models.
The same form appears in maximum-entropy RL and in statistical physics (Boltzmann).
The paper derives this as a known result in the appendix.

items: ELI5. We want a model that earns high reward but does not wander far from what it was. Think of a dog trained with treats on a leash: free to learn, but kept close. The best behaviour has a neat closed form.

Here is the optimisation problem of RLHF's last stage. For each prompt we want a policy that earns high reward, but not at the price of drifting far from the reference. So we maximise the expected reward minus beta times the KL divergence from the reference.

This can be solved exactly. The solution takes the reference distribution and multiplies each response's probability by an exponential factor in its reward. Then it divides by a constant so that probabilities sum to one.
A response with high reward is made more likely, but never to the exclusion of the others, because the reference still contributes.

Look at the two limits of beta. When beta is very large, the exponent is near zero, the factor is near one for every response, and the optimal policy is the reference. When beta is small, the exponent is huge for the best response, and the policy puts nearly all its probability there.
So beta sets a dial between caution and greed.

The trouble is Z of x. It is a sum over every possible response, an astronomically large set for a language model. So we cannot evaluate the optimal policy directly, and RLHF falls back on RL sampling to approach it. DPO instead keeps the formula and uses it algebraically.

practice.title: Optimal policy over a few responses
practice.intro: Write optimal_policy(pi_ref, rewards, beta): the list pi*_i = pi_ref_i * exp(r_i / beta) / Z, rounded to 9 decimals. Use import math.
practice.solution:
import math
def optimal_policy(pi_ref, rewards, beta):
    w = [p * math.exp(r / beta) for p, r in zip(pi_ref, rewards)]
    z = sum(w)
    return [round(x / z, 9) for x in w]

chapters.title: Deriving the DPO loss

maps.title: Derivation
links: Optimal policy | implies | Reward from policy
Reward | equals | Beta log ratio plus log Z
Log Z | depends on | Prompt only
Policy | acts as | A reward model

summary: Take the optimal policy formula and solve it for the reward: r equals beta times the log of the policy over the reference, plus beta times log Z of x. The reward is expressed through the policy.

Substitute into the Bradley-Terry model. The reward gap between the winner and the loser contains log Z of x twice, with opposite signs, so it cancels. The preference probability depends only on the policy and reference.
Maximum likelihood on the observed preferences then gives the DPO loss.

glossary.def: r(x,y) = beta log(pi*(y|x)/pi_ref(y|x)) + beta log Z(x).
log Z(x) appears in both rewards of a pair and drops out of their difference.
r_hat(x,y) = beta log(pi_theta(y|x)/pi_ref(y|x)).
log pi_theta(y|x) - log pi_ref(y|x).
The implicit reward gap between winner and loser.
Given by a formula, without iterative search.

keyPoints: From pi*: r(x,y) = beta log(pi*(y|x)/pi_ref(y|x)) + beta log Z(x).
Gap: r(x,y_w) - r(x,y_l) = beta log(pi*(y_w)/pi_ref(y_w)) - beta log(pi*(y_l)/pi_ref(y_l)).
Z(x) cancels because both responses answer the same prompt.
Replace pi* by the trainable pi_theta and maximise the Bradley-Terry likelihood.
The result is the DPO loss; the policy network is the reward model.
The paper states the language model is secretly a reward model.

items: ELI5. The trick is to rewrite reward using the model itself. Plug that into the preference odds and the reward drops out. What is left is a simple loss: raise the good answer, lower the bad one, relative to the start.

Start from the closed-form optimal policy of the last chapter. Take logarithms and rearrange. The log of the optimal policy equals the log of the reference, plus the reward over beta, minus log Z. Solve for the reward.

This is the key step. It says that any reward function corresponds to an optimal policy, and conversely any policy can be read as defining a reward, up to the term beta log Z of x. That extra term depends on the prompt, not on the response.

Now put this reward into the Bradley-Terry model. The probability of preferring the winner depends on the reward gap between winner and loser, for the same prompt. In the gap, the log Z terms are identical, so they subtract away. The intractable partition function disappears.

lesson.tex: p^{*}(y_w\succ y_l\mid x) \;=\; \sigma\Bigl(\beta\log\frac{\pi^{*}(y_w\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_w\mid x)} - \beta\log\frac{\pi^{*}(y_l\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_l\mid x)}\Bigr)

items: The last step is to treat the policy as the unknown. Replace the optimal policy by a trainable one, and fit it by maximum likelihood on the observed preferences. Minimising the negative log-likelihood gives the DPO loss from chapter 1.
The paper summarises this by saying that the language model is secretly a reward model.

It is worth saying what is assumed. The derivation relies on the Bradley-Terry model being a good description of the preferences, and on the policy class being flexible enough to represent the optimum. Where these fail, DPO and RLHF can differ in practice.
The labs below compute the implicit reward, the margin and the loss.

practice.title: Implicit reward
practice.intro: Write implicit_reward(logp, logp_ref, beta): beta * (logp - logp_ref), rounded to 9 decimals.
practice.solution:
def implicit_reward(logp, logp_ref, beta):
    return round(beta * (logp - logp_ref), 9)

practice.title: Margin
practice.intro: Write margin(lw, lw_ref, ll, ll_ref, beta): the implicit reward of the winner minus that of the loser, rounded to 9 decimals.
practice.solution:
def margin(lw, lw_ref, ll, ll_ref, beta):
    return round(beta * (lw - lw_ref) - beta * (ll - ll_ref), 9)

practice.title: DPO loss for one pair
practice.intro: Write dpo_loss(lw, lw_ref, ll, ll_ref, beta): -ln sigmoid(margin), rounded to 9 decimals. Use import math.
practice.hint: The loss is ln 2 when the margin is zero.

practice.title: Batch loss and accuracy
practice.intro: Write dpo_batch(pairs, beta): pairs is a list of [lw, lw_ref, ll, ll_ref]; return [mean DPO loss, fraction of pairs with a positive margin], both rounded to 9 decimals. Use import math.
practice.solution:
import math
def dpo_batch(pairs, beta):
    tot = 0.0
    ok = 0
    for lw, lwr, ll, llr in pairs:
        m = beta * (lw - lwr) - beta * (ll - llr)
        tot += -math.log(1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-m)))
        if m > 0:
            ok += 1
    n = len(pairs)
    return [round(tot / n, 9), round(ok / n, 9)]

chapters.title: The gradient: who gets updated and how much

maps.title: Gradient
links: Weight | is | Sigmoid of the wrong ordering

summary: Differentiating the DPO loss gives a clean result. For each pair, increase the log-probability of the winner and decrease that of the loser, and scale the step by a weight.
The weight is the sigmoid of the negative margin: large when the implicit reward model ranks the pair wrongly, small when it is already right.
This dynamic weighting is important. The paper reports that a naive version without it, which simply pushes winners up and losers down, can cause the model to degenerate.
The labs compute the weight, the gradient with respect to log-probabilities and one update step on a small table-based policy.

glossary.def: sigma(r_hat_l - r_hat_w): how wrongly the implicit reward orders the pair.
The direction that raises or lowers log pi_theta of a response.
A pair where the loser has the higher implicit reward.
Output quality collapsing when the loss lacks the weighting.
A policy stored as a table of logits, used in the labs.
The size of each gradient step.

keyPoints: grad L = -beta * w * (grad log pi(y_w) - grad log pi(y_l)), averaged over pairs.
w = sigmoid(r_hat(y_l) - r_hat(y_w)) = 1 - sigmoid(margin).
When the margin is large and positive, w is near 0: the pair is already satisfied.
When the margin is negative, w approaches 1: a strong update.
Scaling by beta means larger beta takes larger steps in log-probability, for the same learning rate.
The paper notes the importance of the weight in avoiding degeneration.

items: ELI5. The gradient says: push up the chosen answer and push down the rejected one, harder when the model currently gets the order wrong. Like a teacher who spends more time on the questions you got wrong.

What does a step of DPO do? Differentiate the loss with respect to the policy parameters. The result has a pleasingly interpretable form. It increases the log-probability of the chosen response, it decreases the log-probability of the rejected one, and it multiplies this by a weight.

The weight is the interesting part. It equals the sigmoid of the amount by which the implicit reward model gets the pair wrong. If the model already rates the winner far above the loser, the weight is near zero and the example barely matters.
If the model has the pair backwards, the weight is near one and the example pushes hard.
This focus on mistakes is why DPO behaves sensibly. Easy pairs stop contributing once learned, so training effort goes where the model disagrees with the labels.

The paper also points out that a simpler objective, which just raises winners and lowers losers without this weighting, can make the model degenerate, as nothing stops it from lowering probabilities without limit.
The gradient also shows what beta does. It multiplies the whole expression, and it appears inside the weight through the implicit rewards.

A large beta makes the implicit reward gaps large for a given change in log-probabilities, so the weights fall to zero sooner: the policy stays near the reference. A small beta lets the policy move farther before the pair counts as satisfied.

The labs use a tabular policy, with one logit per response, to see these effects without a neural network. For a softmax over a few candidate responses, the gradient of the log-probability with respect to the logits is the one-hot vector minus the probabilities, as you saw in the PPO course.

practice.title: Gradient weight
practice.intro: Write dpo_weight(margin): sigmoid(-margin), rounded to 9 decimals. Use import math.

practice.title: Logit gradient for one pair
practice.intro: A tabular policy over k candidate responses has logits theta. For a pair (winner index w, loser index l) the gradient of the loss with respect to theta is -beta * weight * ((onehot(w) - p) - (onehot(l) - p)) = -beta * weight * (onehot(w) - onehot(l)), where p is unaffected. Write pair_grad(k, w, l, beta, weight): that list of length k, each rounded to 9 decimals.
practice.hint: Minus beta weight on the winner, plus on the loser.
practice.solution:
def pair_grad(k, w, l, beta, weight):
    g = [0.0] * k
    g[w] = -beta * weight
    g[l] = beta * weight
    return [round(x, 9) for x in g]

practice.title: One DPO step on a tabular policy
practice.intro: A policy over k responses is softmax(theta); the reference is softmax(theta_ref). Write dpo_step(theta, theta_ref, pairs, beta, lr): for each pair [w, l] compute log pi and log pi_ref (log of the softmax probabilities), margin = beta*((lp_w - ref_w) - (lp_l - ref_l)), weight = sigmoid(-margin); the gradient of the loss with respect to the logits uses the full softmax gradients: -beta*weight*((onehot(w)-p) - (onehot(l)-p)) = -beta*weight*(onehot(w)-onehot(l)). Average over the pairs and return theta minus lr times that average, rounded to 6 decimals. Use import math.
practice.hint: Raise the winner's logit, lower the loser's, weighted.
practice.solution:
import math
def dpo_step(theta, theta_ref, pairs, beta, lr):
    def logsm(t):
        m = max(t)
        s = sum(math.exp(x - m) for x in t)
        return [x - m - math.log(s) for x in t]
    lp = logsm(theta)
    lr_ref = logsm(theta_ref)
    k = len(theta)
    g = [0.0] * k
    for w, l in pairs:
        margin = beta * ((lp[w] - lr_ref[w]) - (lp[l] - lr_ref[l]))
        weight = 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(margin))
        g[w] += -beta * weight
        g[l] += beta * weight
    n = len(pairs)
    return [round(theta[i] - lr * g[i] / n, 6) for i in range(k)]

chapters.title: Implementing DPO: sequences, batches and practicalities
summary: A response is a sequence of tokens. Its log-probability is the sum of the log-probabilities of its tokens given the prompt and the earlier tokens. DPO needs this sum for the chosen and the rejected response under both the policy and the reference.
Prompt tokens must be masked, so that only response tokens contribute. Reference log-probabilities do not change, so they can be computed once and stored.
In the paper's experiments beta of 0.1 was a typical value. Learning rates are small, since the policy starts near the reference. A supervised fine-tuning stage usually comes first.

glossary.def: The sum over response tokens of log pi(token | context).
Excluding prompt (and padding) tokens from the sum.
Calculating reference log-probabilities once before training.
Supervised fine-tuning, usually done before DPO.
A typical value is 0.1; chosen by experiment.
A tendency for sums of log-probabilities to favour shorter or longer responses.

keyPoints: log pi(y|x) = sum over response tokens of log pi(y_t | x, y_<t).
Only response tokens count; prompt and padding are masked.
Reference log-probabilities can be precomputed once.
Common beta about 0.1 (the paper explores 0.1 to 0.5 in places); tuned per task.
DPO usually starts from a supervised fine-tuned model that also serves as the reference.
Longer responses have lower total log-probability, which can interact with the loss.

items: ELI5. In practice each answer is a sequence of words, so we add up the log-probability of every word. Batches hold many pairs, and a frozen copy of the starting model gives the baseline.

So far we treated a response as a single item with a probability. A real response is a sequence of tokens. By the chain rule of probability, the probability of the whole response is the product of the token probabilities, each conditioned on the prompt and the tokens before.
Taking logs turns the product into a sum.

In code, run the model on the concatenated prompt and response once. It outputs a distribution over the vocabulary at each position. Pick out the log-probability of the actual next token at each response position.
Mask out the prompt positions, since the prompt is given, not generated, and padding positions. Sum what remains.
Each training step needs four such sums: the policy and the reference, for the chosen and the rejected response. The reference model is frozen, so its sums never change.
A common saving is to compute them once before training and store them with the data, so the reference need not be in memory during the updates.

Practical advice from the paper and common implementations: begin from a model already fine-tuned on good responses, and use that same model as the reference. Use a small learning rate, since a large one will quickly leave the neighbourhood where the reference is a sensible anchor.
Beta of 0.1 is a common starting value. Larger values keep the model closer.

One known subtlety is length. A longer response has a more negative total log-probability simply because it has more tokens, so the log-ratios can interact with length. Several later methods normalise by length. I come back to this in the chapter on variants.
The labs compute sequence log-probabilities with masks and build one batch of DPO inputs.

chapters.title: Choosing beta and understanding behaviour

maps.title: Behaviour
links: Off-policy data | can mismatch | The reference

summary: Beta is the most important knob. Small beta lets the policy move far from the reference, which can give larger gains and more risk. Large beta keeps it close. The right value depends on the data and the model.

DPO is trained offline on a fixed set of pairs. If the responses came from another model, the reference may give them very low probability. Many practitioners therefore fine-tune on the preferred responses first.

A reported effect, sometimes called likelihood displacement, is that DPO can lower the probability of both the chosen and the rejected response, so long as the gap grows. This is background knowledge from later analyses.

glossary.def: Chosen and rejected log-probabilities both fall while their gap grows.
Learning from a fixed dataset without sampling new responses.
Mismatch between the data and what the model would generate.
The share of comparisons in which one model's response is preferred.
Fitting the training pairs too closely; the margin keeps growing.
The share of pairs with a positive implicit reward margin.

keyPoints: Larger beta keeps the policy closer to the reference.
Training on pairs not generated by the reference can cause distribution shift.
Margins can grow without bound; with noisy labels this overfits.
Both chosen and rejected log-probs may decline (later analyses; background).
Track: loss, reward accuracy, margin, chosen/rejected rewards, KL to reference.
Final evaluation uses held-out prompts and win rates against a baseline.

items: ELI5. Beta is a knob for how tightly the leash is held. Small beta lets the model move far; large beta keeps it near the start. Too loose and it may drift; too tight and it learns nothing.

Consider the roles of beta again. In the loss, beta multiplies the log-ratio. In the optimal policy it sets the temperature of the reward tilt. A small beta says: I trust the preference data, and I let the policy drift. A large beta says: stay close.
The paper's experiments use values such as 0.1 and compare behaviour as the KL to the reference grows.

DPO trains offline on a fixed dataset, so the data matters a great deal. Suppose the responses came from a very different model. Then under the reference both may be very unlikely, and the log-ratios behave strangely.
A common remedy, noted in the paper, is to first fine-tune the reference on the preferred responses.

A further effect has been described in later analyses. The loss only cares about the gap between chosen and rejected. It can be reduced by lowering the rejected probability a lot while lowering the chosen one a little. So both probabilities can fall.
Some observers call this likelihood displacement. Variants add a term that keeps the chosen likelihood up. I mark this as background knowledge, not a result of the original paper.

Overfitting is another risk. With a clean dataset the margin can be increased without limit by driving the loser's probability toward zero. With noisy labels this memorises noise. Early stopping, a larger beta, a smaller learning rate or label smoothing can all help.
To monitor training, log the loss, the reward accuracy, the average margin, the implicit rewards of the chosen and rejected responses, and an estimate of the KL divergence to the reference.
For the final judgement use held-out prompts and compare responses against a baseline, by human raters or by a model judge, and report the win rate.

practice.title: Optimal policy for a given beta
practice.intro: With two responses, reference probabilities p_ref = [0.5, 0.5] and rewards [1.0, 0.0], write prob_best(beta): the optimal policy's probability on the first response, rounded to 9 decimals. Use import math.

practice.title: Diagnostics
practice.intro: Write diagnostics(margins, chosen_rewards, rejected_rewards): return [reward accuracy (fraction of margins above 0), mean margin, mean chosen reward, mean rejected reward], each rounded to 9 decimals.
practice.solution:
def diagnostics(margins, chosen_rewards, rejected_rewards):
    n = len(margins)
    acc = sum(1 for m in margins if m > 0) / n
    return [round(acc, 9), round(sum(margins) / n, 9), round(sum(chosen_rewards) / n, 9), round(sum(rejected_rewards) / n, 9)]

practice.title: Displacement check
practice.intro: Write displaced(chosen_before, chosen_after, rejected_before, rejected_after): True if the chosen log-prob fell AND the gap (chosen minus rejected) grew.
practice.solution:
def displaced(chosen_before, chosen_after, rejected_before, rejected_after):
    gap_before = chosen_before - rejected_before
    gap_after = chosen_after - rejected_after
    return chosen_after < chosen_before and gap_after > gap_before

chapters.title: Variants, relatives and where DPO fits
summary: DPO started a family. IPO modifies the loss to avoid overfitting. KTO works with thumbs-up or thumbs-down labels on single responses. ORPO combines supervised fine-tuning and preference learning without a reference model. SimPO uses length-normalised log-probabilities.
Online versions sample fresh responses during training. GRPO keeps the reinforcement learning loop but replaces the value model by group statistics.
All of these are later work and are background knowledge in this course. Details differ and evidence about which is best is mixed; treat comparisons with some care.
The labs implement small versions of three of these ideas.

glossary.def: Identity Preference Optimization: squared-error loss on the margin, aimed at reducing overfitting.
Kahneman-Tversky Optimization: learns from labels on single responses.
Odds Ratio Preference Optimization: no reference model.
Simple Preference Optimization: average log-probability as the reward.
DPO with fresh samples from the current policy, labelled by a judge.
Group Relative Policy Optimization: PPO-like with group-normalised advantages.

keyPoints: IPO: loss = (margin_in_logratio - 1/(2 tau))^2 style regression to a target gap.
SimPO: reward = beta / |y| * log pi(y|x), with a target margin gamma.
KTO: needs only 'good' or 'bad' labels per response.
ORPO: adds an odds-ratio penalty to the SFT loss; no reference model.
Online methods reduce distribution shift by sampling from the current policy.
These variants are later than the DPO paper; evidence on which is best is mixed.

items: ELI5. DPO has relatives: variants that change the loss or use other data. They all try to learn from preferences with less machinery. DPO sits between plain fine-tuning and full reinforcement learning.
DPO's simplicity made it popular, and its limits prompted many variants. Here is a map, with the usual warning that this is the fast-moving part of the field.

IPO changes the loss from log-sigmoid to a squared error pushing the margin toward a fixed target. The aim is to stop the margin from growing without limit when labels are very consistent, which curbs overfitting.

KTO is designed for data where you only have thumbs-up or thumbs-down on single responses rather than pairs. ORPO folds preference learning into supervised fine-tuning with an odds-ratio term, and does not need a reference model, saving memory.
SimPO scores a response by its average, not total, log-probability, which treats length more evenly.

A different line addresses the offline nature of DPO. Online or iterative DPO samples new responses from the current policy, has a judge rank them, trains on the new pairs, and repeats. This removes the distribution shift, but brings back a sampling loop, which was what DPO aimed to avoid.
Seen this way, PPO-style RLHF and DPO sit at two ends of a spectrum.

GRPO keeps online reinforcement learning but drops the value model: for each prompt it samples a group of responses, and the advantage of each is its reward minus the group mean, divided by the group standard deviation. It has been popular for reasoning models trained with verifiable rewards.

How to choose? DPO is a strong default when you have a good preference dataset and limited compute. PPO-like methods give more control when you have a reliable reward signal and can afford sampling. Whatever you pick, evaluate on held-out prompts.
Where to go next: read the DPO paper, then try the loss on a small open model with a preference dataset, and plot the diagnostics from chapter 7.

practice.title: IPO-style loss
practice.intro: Write ipo_loss(margin_logratio, tau): the squared error (margin_logratio - 1 / (2 * tau)) ** 2, where margin_logratio is the winner minus loser log-ratio (without beta). Round to 9 decimals.
practice.hint: Regress the gap to a target.
practice.solution:
def ipo_loss(margin_logratio, tau):
    return round((margin_logratio - 1.0 / (2.0 * tau)) ** 2, 9)

practice.title: SimPO reward
practice.intro: Write simpo_reward(logp_sum, length, beta): beta * logp_sum / length, rounded to 9 decimals.
practice.solution:
def simpo_reward(logp_sum, length, beta):
    return round(beta * logp_sum / length, 9)

practice.title: SimPO loss
practice.intro: Write simpo_loss(lp_w, len_w, lp_l, len_l, beta, gamma): -ln sigmoid(reward_w - reward_l - gamma) using the SimPO reward, rounded to 9 decimals. Use import math.

practice.title: Group advantages
practice.intro: Write group_advantages(rewards): the GRPO-style advantage of each sampled response, (reward - mean) / (std + 1e-8) with population std, rounded to 6 decimals. Use import math.
practice.solution:
import math
def group_advantages(rewards):
    n = len(rewards)
    mu = sum(rewards) / n
    var = sum((r - mu) ** 2 for r in rewards) / n
    s = math.sqrt(var)
    return [round((r - mu) / (s + 1e-8), 6) for r in rewards]
